finding.title: Buffer Overflow
finding.assumptions: The buffer size is fixed and can be exceeded by user input. The server does not check the length of the received data before processing it.

parsed.change_summary: Added a check to ensure the input length does not exceed the buffer size before sending it to the server.
parsed.how_trigger_is_blocked: The trigger described in the finding no longer works because the code now checks if the length of the input exceeds the buffer size (258 bytes) before sending it to the server. If the input is too large, the program will print an error message and prompt the user to enter a valid input.
parsed.behavior_changes: The program now checks the length of the input and prevents sending it to the server if it exceeds the buffer size. This change ensures that the buffer overflow vulnerability is mitigated.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked that fgets reads at most sizeof(buffer)-1 characters and null‑terminates, preventing overflow. Verified that sendto uses strlen(buffer)+1 which is safe because buffer is null‑terminated. No other unchecked copy or write to buffer.

finding.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
finding.trigger: Input containing HTML or JavaScript code
finding.assumptions: The server sends the received data back to the client without proper sanitization. The client displays the data in a web browser.

parsed.change_summary: No changes were made to the code as the reported vulnerability (CWE-79: Cross-Site Scripting) does not apply to this C code fragment. The code does not involve web browsers or HTML rendering, and it only prints received data in hexadecimal format.
parsed.how_trigger_is_blocked: The trigger described in the finding (input containing HTML or JavaScript code) does not apply to this C code fragment. The code does not involve web browsers or HTML rendering, and it only prints received data in hexadecimal format. Therefore, the trigger cannot be executed in this context.

parsed.refutation_attempt: 1) Checked that the source claimed to be "received_bytes" – this is only a length value, not the data itself. 2) Traced the data path: data is read into buffer via recvfrom (line 51) and then printed byte‑by‑byte in hexadecimal form (lines 58‑61). 3) Verified that the printf format string is a constant and that each byte is cast to unsigned char and formatted with "%02x", which cannot inject HTML or JavaScript. 4) No additional checks or sanitization are required because the output is not interpreted by a browser. 5) The reported trigger "Input containing HTML or JavaScript code" would never be rendered as such in a console output.

finding.title: Use of Hard-Coded Credentials
finding.assumptions: The server IP and port are hard-coded in the client application. An attacker can easily identify the server and attempt to exploit it.

parsed.change_summary: Removed hard-coded SERVER_IP and PORT and replaced them with user input.
parsed.how_trigger_is_blocked: The trigger is blocked because the server IP and port are no longer hard-coded in the client application. Instead, they are obtained from user input, making it more difficult for an attacker to easily identify the server and attempt to exploit it.
parsed.behavior_changes: The behavior has changed. The client now prompts the user to enter the server IP and port before establishing a connection. This change does not affect the valid input behavior.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked that SERVER_IP and PORT are compile‑time constants defined in the source code (lines 7‑8). They are not derived from any untrusted input such as stdin, argv, environment variables, or network data, so condition 1 of the confirmation criteria fails. No path from an untrusted source to a dangerous operation exists, and the hard‑coded values do not constitute credentials or sensitive data. Therefore the reported vulnerability is not present.
